5260:
Enduring means lasting for a very long time, often despite the passage of time, changing trends, or difficult circumstances.

When you call something enduring, you are saying two things at once:

  1. It has already lasted a long time.
  2. It shows no sign of weakening or disappearing.

Think of it this way: if something is enduring, time has tried to wear it down — and failed.

"Enduring" almost always carries a positive or admiring tone. It implies strength, depth, and resilience. When you describe something as enduring, you are quietly paying it a compliment — you are saying it has proven itself worthy of surviving.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "They have an old friendship."
  • "They have an enduring friendship."

Both say the friendship is old. But the second one says something more: that this friendship has held up, remained strong, and stood the test of time. It feels more powerful and meaningful.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is where learners often get confused, so let's be precise.

Enduring vs. Lasting — These are very close. "Lasting" simply means something continues for a long time. "Enduring" goes one step further — it quietly suggests the thing has earned its survival, that something about it is strong enough to resist being forgotten or erased. "Enduring" feels slightly richer and more impressive than "lasting."

Enduring vs. Permanent — "Permanent" means something will never end. "Enduring" does not make that claim. An enduring friendship could theoretically end one day — but it has lasted remarkably long and remains strong right now. "Permanent" is absolute; "enduring" is deeply long-lasting, but not necessarily forever.

Enduring vs. Timeless — "Timeless" means something feels like it belongs to no particular era — it never goes out of style. "Enduring" means something has actually survived across time and is still going strong. A song can be timeless because it feels fresh forever. A friendship is enduring because it has genuinely lasted through years of real life.

Seeing a word in different situations is the best way to truly understand it.

In relationships:
"Their enduring love for each other inspired everyone around them."
→ A love that stayed strong across many years, probably through hardships too.

In ideas and culture:
"Shakespeare's works have an enduring appeal."
→ Even after 400+ years, people still read and love Shakespeare. His appeal has not faded.

In impact:
"The scientist left an enduring legacy in the field of medicine."
→ Her contributions did not vanish after she died. They continue to influence the field today.

In memory:
"The photograph became an enduring image of the war."
→ The image is so powerful that people have never forgotten it, even decades later.

In problems (neutral use):
"Poverty remains an enduring challenge for many nations."
→ Here, "enduring" simply means the problem has persisted for a very long time. The word itself is neutral, even though the subject is negative.

This last example shows something important: "enduring" describes the quality of lasting long — not whether the thing itself is good or bad. It is most commonly used in positive contexts, but it can describe anything that has proven long-lasting.

• It does not mean something that is simply old or ancient. An old building is not automatically enduring — it is enduring only if it has held up well and remains significant or strong.
  • It does not mean permanent or eternal. It means remarkably long-lasting, not everlasting.
  • It is not the same as "popular." Something can be popular for a short time (a trend). Something enduring stays relevant and strong far beyond what is typical.

"Enduring" most naturally appears before certain nouns. Learning these pairings will help you use the word naturally:

Enduring love / enduring friendship / enduring bond — relationships that have stood the test of time.
Enduring legacy / enduring impact / enduring influence — the long-lasting effect someone or something leaves behind.
Enduring appeal / enduring popularity — the ability to attract admiration or interest across a long period.
Enduring symbol / enduring image / enduring memory — something so powerful it is never forgotten.
Enduring mystery / enduring problem / enduring question — something that has persisted without being solved or resolved.

If you need to remember just one thing: enduring means something has lasted a remarkably long time and continues to remain strong, meaningful, or relevant — having quietly proven its worth against the test of time.
5261:
To energize something or someone means to fill them with energy, making them active, lively, powerful, or ready to act.

Think of it like charging a battery. A dead battery does nothing. A charged battery powers things. When you energize something, you are essentially "charging" it — giving it the force, drive, or power it needs to move, work, or come alive.
The Two Main Senses

Sense 1 — Giving a person (or group) emotional/physical energy

This is the most everyday use of the word. When something energizes you, it makes you feel awake, motivated, excited, and ready to take on the world. It removes mental or physical sluggishness and replaces it with vigor and enthusiasm.

  • A good night's sleep energized her for the long day ahead.
  • The coach's speech energized the team before the final match.
  • Listening to loud music energizes him when he works out.
  • The new project completely energized the staff — everyone seemed more excited and productive.

Notice that in all these cases, something is acting on a person, pumping them full of drive and vitality.

Sense 2 — Supplying electrical or physical power to a system or device

In technical or scientific contexts, energize means to supply electricity or power to something so it becomes active or operational.

  • The switch energizes the circuit, allowing current to flow.
  • The solar panels energize the entire building.
  • Press the button to energize the motor.

Here, the word is more literal — you are literally sending energy (electrical, mechanical) into something so it functions.
One Word, One Idea at Heart

Although the two senses seem different (one is emotional, one is physical/electrical), they are really the same idea at the core: taking something that was inactive, dull, or powerless and giving it the energy to function or flourish. The word bridges the human and the mechanical beautifully.
What Can Energize Something?

Almost anything can serve as the "source" of energizing:

  • Physical things: exercise, food, sleep, coffee, sunlight
  • Emotional/social things: praise, music, a great conversation, a new challenge, good news
  • Ideas or events: a powerful speech, a breakthrough idea, a competition
  • Electrical sources: a battery, a generator, a power grid
What Can Be Energized?

• People and animals — they feel motivated, alert, or physically revived
  • Groups and crowds — a whole team, an audience, a workforce
  • Machines and systems — circuits, motors, devices
  • Abstract things — a discussion can be energized (made more lively), a market can be energized (made more active), a brand can be energized (given fresh life)
The Feeling It Describes

When a person is energized, they typically feel:

  • Alert and awake (not sluggish or tired)
  • Motivated and eager to act
  • Excited or enthusiastic
  • Capable and strong

It is a positive, uplifting feeling. The word almost always carries a good connotation — being energized is desirable.
Passive Form: "Be Energized"

You will often see this word used in the passive form.

  • I feel energized after that run. (The run gave me energy.)
  • She was energized by the crowd's applause.
  • The workers were energized by the new leadership.

In passive form, the focus is on the person receiving the energy boost rather than on who or what caused it.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Motivate — To motivate someone is to give them a reason or desire to do something. It is about direction (why you should act). Energize is about power (the fuel to act). You can feel motivated but still tired; being energized means you actually feel the physical or emotional readiness.

Invigorate — Very close in meaning. To invigorate is to make someone feel strong, healthy, and full of life — often used for physical freshness (a cold shower invigorates). Energize is slightly broader and can apply to motivational and technical contexts too.

Stimulate — To stimulate is to cause activity or growth, often by triggering a reaction. It is more neutral and clinical. Energize is warmer and implies filling something up with vitality or enthusiasm.

Excite — Excitement is about heightened emotion, sometimes including nervousness or anticipation. Energize specifically refers to the power and readiness to act, not just the emotional state. Being energized is calmer and more purposeful than being excited.
Strength and Intensity of the Word

Energize is a strong, active word. It implies a noticeable, meaningful boost — not a tiny nudge. If something barely helps you, you would not typically say it energized you. The word suggests a real surge of power, drive, or life.
Negation: When Energy is Drained

The word is typically used positively, but context can show its absence:

  • Nothing seemed to energize the crowd. (The crowd stayed flat and lifeless.)
  • The meeting failed to energize the team. (It left everyone unmoved or even more tired.)
Summary in One Line
To energize = to give (a person, group, machine, or system) the energy, power, or vitality it needs to become active, lively, or effective — whether that energy is emotional, physical, or electrical.
5262:
To enervate someone means to drain them of strength, energy, or vitality — to leave them feeling weakened, listless, and depleted. When something enervates you, it doesn't just make you ordinarily tired. It empties you out. It strips away your drive, your sharpness, your will to act. Think of it like a slow leak in a tire: the tire isn't suddenly flat, but the air — the life — has been quietly drained away.

The key idea is removal. Something acts on a person from the outside and saps their vigor. Heat enervates. Illness enervates. A soul-crushing routine enervates. Chronic stress enervates. A toxic environment enervates.
The critical mistake most people make

This is the single most important thing to know about this word, so pay close attention: many people — including educated ones — mistakenly believe "enervate" means to energize or to fill with vigor. This is completely wrong, and it is the exact opposite of what the word means. The confusion likely happens because the word vaguely resembles "energize" or "invigorate." Don't fall for this trap. Enervate means to weaken and drain, never to charge up or empower.
What being enervated actually feels like

Enervation is deeper than ordinary tiredness. Tiredness usually implies you'll recover after some rest. To be enervated suggests something more serious has been leached away — your mental sharpness, your motivation, your moral or emotional resilience. A person who is enervated feels apathetic, languid, perhaps even unable to summon the will to resist or react. The word carries a sense of hollowness.
What kinds of things can enervate someone?

Almost anything that slowly saps a person's strength can be described as enervating. Oppressive heat or humidity. A prolonged illness. Years of monotonous, joyless work. An exhausting relationship. Chronic anxiety. Even excessive comfort and luxury can be described as enervating in a moral or intellectual sense — the idea being that a life of ease can gradually drain a person's sharpness and discipline. This more figurative use appears often in literature and formal writing.

"The relentless summer heat enervated the soldiers well before they reached the battlefield." Here, the heat is the agent doing the draining, and the soldiers are the ones being weakened.

"Years of bureaucratic red tape had enervated what was once a bold and creative team." Here, a situation — the grinding routine — has slowly drained the team's vitality.

"She emerged from the illness feeling deeply enervated, unable to concentrate for more than a few minutes." Here, the past-tense form "enervated" functions as an adjective describing her state.

"The endless, repetitive meetings had an enervating effect on everyone in the department." Here, "enervating" is used as an adjective modifying "effect."
The different forms of the word you'll encounter

Enervate is the base verb: "Prolonged isolation can enervate the human spirit."

Enervated is both the past tense of the verb and a common adjective: "He returned from the expedition enervated and gaunt."

Enervating is the present participle, also used widely as an adjective: "The enervating humidity made any outdoor activity feel pointless."

Enervation is the noun form — the state or condition of being enervated: "A deep enervation had settled over the troops after months in the field."
How it compares to similar words

Tire and exhaust are everyday cousins of "enervate," but they are simpler and more physical. "Enervate" is more formal and tends to describe a deeper, more lasting depletion — often of the mind, spirit, or will, not just the body.

Debilitate is close and can overlap, but it leans more toward physical weakness caused by disease or injury. "Enervate" is broader in scope.

Sap (as in, "it sapped his strength") is informal but captures a similar idea — a slow draining away. "Enervate" is its more elevated, formal equivalent.

The antonyms — words meaning the opposite — are invigorate, energize, fortify, and vitalize.
The overall feel of the word

"Enervate" belongs to formal, literary, and academic writing. You won't often hear it in casual conversation, but you will encounter it in novels, essays, journalism, and professional contexts. When a writer chooses "enervate" over "tire" or "drain," they are signaling something deliberate — that the weakening is gradual, significant, and cuts deeper than mere physical fatigue. It often implies that something valuable — ambition, spirit, creativity, resilience — has been quietly stolen away.
5263:
Enervating describes something that drains your energy, strength, and vitality, leaving you feeling weak, limp, and depleted. It describes the cause of that drained feeling — not the feeling itself.

When you call something enervating, you are saying: this thing is sucking the life out of me.
The most important thing to know: don't be fooled

This word tricks almost everyone at first, because it sounds like it should mean "energizing." It does not. It means the complete opposite.

  • Energizing → something that gives you energy. ✅
  • Enervating → something that takes away your energy. ✅

Memorize this contrast, and you've already won half the battle with this word.

Being tired after a run is not quite what "enervating" captures. "Enervating" points to something deeper — a heavy, total kind of depletion that affects your body, your mind, and your will all at once. It's the feeling of being drained hollow. Limp. Listless. Without the desire or ability to do much of anything.

Think of these situations:

  • You've spent hours under blazing, humid summer heat. You haven't done any real physical work, yet your body feels leaden, your thoughts have gone sluggish, and even lifting your arm feels like an effort.
  • You've sat through a four-hour meeting where nothing meaningful was discussed. By the end, you feel mentally empty — not just bored, but genuinely sapped of something.
  • You've spent weeks in a tense, conflict-ridden environment. You haven't been physically active, yet you feel utterly worn down and spiritless.

All of these are enervating experiences. Notice that the depletion can be physical, mental, emotional, or all three at once. What they all share is this: something outside of you has weakened you from within.
What kinds of things can be "enervating"?

The word is flexible. It can describe situations, environments, conditions, work, weather, people, or experiences — essentially anything that acts as a drain on your energy or spirit.

Here are examples across different contexts:

Weather: "The enervating August heat left the entire city moving in slow motion."

Work or routine: "Years of repetitive, purposeless work had an enervating effect on his motivation."

Illness: "The enervating fatigue that came with the illness was harder to bear than the pain itself."

Emotional atmosphere: "Growing up in that tense household was deeply enervating — she was always exhausted without knowing why."

Processes and systems: "The enervating bureaucracy of renewing the permit — form after form, office after office — drained her completely."

People: "He was an enervating presence; every conversation with him left her feeling strangely hollow."

"Enervating" sits in the range between tiring and debilitating, but it leans closer to the serious end. It suggests more than mild fatigue — it implies a meaningful loss of vitality and vigor. However, it doesn't usually suggest complete physical collapse (that would be closer to "incapacitating" or "prostrating").

Think of it as: significantly and deeply draining, in a way that weakens your whole being.

Draining, exhausting, debilitating, sapping, wearying, devitalizing, weakening.

The key distinction: "enervating" is slightly more literary and formal than simply saying "tiring" or "draining." It also carries a more specific sense — it isn't just that you feel tired; it's that something has weakened you, stripped away your vigor and will.
How formal is this word, and where will you see it?

"Enervating" is a formal, literary word. You'll encounter it most often in novels, essays, literary journalism, and thoughtful writing. In casual everyday conversation, people tend to say "draining" or "exhausting" instead. But when a writer chooses "enervating," they are being very precise — they want you to feel that specific sense of deep, depleting weakness, not just garden-variety tiredness.

Whenever you're tempted to confuse it with "energizing," picture a vampire. An energizing thing is like sunlight — it fills you up. An enervating thing is like a vampire — it finds you full of life and leaves you drained. Enervating = the vampire of experiences.
Enervating describes anything that drains your energy and weakens your vitality, leaving you feeling depleted, limp, and without vigor — the opposite of invigorating.
5264:
Enervation means a profound state of weakness, depletion, and drained vitality — physical, mental, or both. It describes the condition of having your energy, strength, or willpower sapped out of you, leaving you limp, listless, and unable to function at your normal capacity.

Think of it like a battery that has been almost completely drained. The battery still exists, but it has almost nothing left to give. That is the state of enervation.

Enervation is not just being tired. It is deeper than that. When someone is in a state of enervation, they feel:

  • A heavy, almost suffocating weakness in both body and mind
  • A complete unwillingness or inability to act or exert themselves
  • A sense of listlessness — where even the thought of doing something feels overwhelming
  • A hollowed-out quality, as if the life force inside them has been quietly drained away

A tired person rests and feels better in an hour. A person experiencing enervation may rest and still feel hollow, weak, and utterly depleted. It carries a sense of being thoroughly worn down over time, not just momentarily fatigued.
The Single Most Important Thing to Know About This Word

This is a trap that catches almost everyone: enervation sounds like "energy," but it means the complete opposite.

Because the word begins with "ener-", people instinctively assume it has something to do with giving or increasing energy. It does not. Enervation is the removal or draining of energy and strength. It is the state of being left without vigor.

If someone says "the speech caused enervation in the crowd," it means the crowd was left feeling drained and weakened — not inspired or energized. Keeping this reversal firmly in mind is the key to using and understanding this word correctly.

The noun enervation comes directly from the verb enervate, which means to weaken or drain someone of energy and vitality. The relationship is simple:

  • To enervate = the action of draining strength from someone or something
  • Enervation = the resulting state of having been drained

So, a scorching summer day might enervate you → and the weakness you feel afterward is enervation.

Enervation can be brought about by many things, and understanding its causes helps cement the meaning:

  • Extreme heat — a sweltering, humid day can strip a person of all physical motivation and strength
  • Prolonged illness — a long sickness slowly drains a person until they are left in a state of enervation
  • Chronic stress or overwork — grinding, relentless pressure over weeks or months depletes a person mentally and physically
  • Overindulgence — too much alcohol, food, or luxury can paradoxically leave a person feeling weakened and inert
  • A deeply demoralizing experience — a crushing disappointment or humiliation can enervate a person mentally, leaving their spirit weakened

What these causes share in common is that they take something away from the person. They drain. They deplete. They hollow out. That is the essence of what produces enervation.

Enervation can apply to the body, the mind, or both simultaneously.

Physical enervation is the bodily version — your muscles feel weak, your limbs feel heavy, your body refuses to cooperate. Imagine someone who has just recovered from a fever. They may be technically "better," but they stand up and feel wobbly, drained, and feeble. That physical depletion is enervation.

Mental enervation is the psychological version — your mind feels sluggish, your motivation has evaporated, your ability to think clearly or make decisions feels impaired. A person who has spent months in a grinding, thankless job might reach a point of mental enervation, where they sit at their desk and feel completely hollowed out of any drive or clarity.

Often, the two come together — a physically enervated body drags down the mind, and a mentally enervated mind makes the body feel heavy.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Many words overlap with enervation, but each has a slightly different flavour:

Tiredness / Fatigue — these are common, everyday words for needing rest. Enervation is more severe, more complete, and implies a deeper hollowing-out than simple tiredness. You are tired after a workout. You experience enervation after months of illness.

Exhaustion — this is close to enervation in intensity, but exhaustion tends to suggest you have used up all your energy through effort or exertion. Enervation suggests your energy has been drained from you, often without you even doing much. The distinction is subtle but real: exhaustion is spending everything; enervation is having everything taken.

Lethargy — lethargy is a sluggish, heavy reluctance to do anything. It overlaps with enervation but is slightly narrower — it focuses on the sluggishness of movement and motivation. Enervation is the broader state that often causes lethargy.

Debilitation — this word is the closest cousin. Debilitation means a severe weakening that impairs normal functioning, and enervation sits very comfortably beside it. If anything, enervation is slightly more evocative and literary, while debilitation is more clinical and neutral.

Seeing the word used naturally is the final step in truly owning it:

  • "The weeks of chemotherapy left her in a state of enervation so deep that she struggled to sit up in bed."
  • "The tropical humidity produced a creeping enervation in the tourists — by noon, nobody wanted to do anything but lie still."
  • "There is a particular enervation that comes not from hard work, but from meaningless work — a soul-level draining that sleep cannot fix."
  • "The defeat was not just disappointing; it caused a kind of enervation in the team that lasted for weeks."

In strict medical and anatomical contexts, enervation can also refer to the cutting or removal of a nerve from a part of the body — literally depriving tissue of its nerve supply. This is a technical, specialized usage you will mostly encounter in medical literature. The everyday meaning — the state of profound weakness and depletion described above — is by far the more common one, and the one you will encounter in literature, journalism, and general conversation.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: Enervation is the state of being drained of energy and strength — a deep, hollow weakness of body, mind, or both — caused by forces that slowly or suddenly sap your vitality away.
5265:
"Enfant terrible" is a French phrase that English borrowed directly and uses as its own. In French, enfant means "child" and terrible means "terrible" or "dreadful." So the literal translation is simply "terrible child" or "dreadful child."

How to pronounce it: ahn-fahn teh-REE-bluh. Both words carry a soft, nasal French sound. In English conversation, people often say it with a loose approximation: on-fon teh-REE-bul. Either is understood and acceptable.

The phrase began with a very specific, literal image: a young child who says or does embarrassing things in front of adults — especially in public or social situations.

Picture a family at a formal dinner party. The adults are being polite and careful with their words. Then the seven-year-old blurts out, "Why is Uncle Pierre so fat?" or "Mummy, you told Papa you hated these people!" — something completely true, but mortifying to say aloud.

That child — innocent, unfiltered, oblivious to social rules — was the original enfant terrible. There was no malice in the child. The horror came from the child's complete freedom from the invisible fences that adults build around themselves.

This original sense still exists. If someone says a child is an enfant terrible in a literal context, they mean the child is a handful — unpredictable, outspoken, and embarrassing to be around in polite company.

Over time, people noticed something interesting about that blunt, rule-ignoring child: they were often right. The child said what everyone was thinking but was too afraid to say. The child disrupted a comfortable but false social peace by telling the truth.

This led to a shift. The phrase began to be applied not just to children, but to adults — particularly artists, writers, designers, filmmakers, musicians, and thinkers — who behaved with that same child-like disregard for rules, conventions, and what is "supposed to be done."

These adults were shocking. They provoked people. They broke established norms in their fields. They said and did things that made their peers uncomfortable. But crucially, they were talented, original, and often turned out to be ahead of their time.

The meaning gradually transformed from a simple insult into something more complicated — almost a backhanded compliment.
What It Means Today (The Core Modern Usage)

Today, when someone is called an enfant terrible, it almost always refers to a creative, bold, unconventional person — usually in the arts, fashion, film, literature, or business — who deliberately breaks rules, defies expectations, and provokes controversy, yet is respected or even celebrated for their talent and originality.

The label carries these qualities together:

Rebellious. They don't follow the rules of their industry or field. They challenge what is accepted, normal, or expected.

Provocative. They say, make, or do things that shock people, stir debate, or make people uncomfortable. They are not interested in playing it safe.

Talented. This is crucial. The term is not used for someone who is merely rude or difficult. The enfant terrible has genuine ability. Their rule-breaking comes from creative vision, not ignorance.

Young (or young in spirit). The label most naturally fits people who are either literally young in their career, or who carry a youthful fearlessness regardless of their age — that same unfiltered boldness of the child at the dinner table.

Simultaneously admired and criticized. People around them are often irritated, scandalized, or offended. And yet they cannot look away. The enfant terrible commands attention precisely because they do what no one else dares.
The Tone: Is It an Insult or a Compliment?

This is where the phrase gets genuinely interesting.

It is both, at once. The tone depends heavily on who is using it and in what spirit.

If a traditional, conservative figure calls someone an enfant terrible, they likely mean it with at least some disapproval — the person is too wild, too disruptive, too difficult to manage.

But in many modern contexts — especially in journalism, arts criticism, and popular culture — being called an enfant terrible is worn as a badge of honour. It signals that you are daring enough to challenge the establishment, original enough to be noticed, and talented enough that people take your provocation seriously rather than dismissing it.

Think of it this way: nobody calls a forgettable, mediocre, rule-following person an enfant terrible. The label is reserved for those who matter enough to disturb people.
Who Gets Called an Enfant Terrible?

The label has been applied across many fields:

In fashion: A young designer who tears apart decades of tradition and creates something that looks almost offensive — until the rest of the industry copies it five years later.

In film: A director who makes deeply uncomfortable, unconventional movies that critics argue about furiously, but which become landmarks of cinema.

In literature: A young writer whose novel breaks every rule of "good writing" but captures something raw and true that polished, rule-following books miss entirely.

In music: A performer who shocks audiences with provocative performances, is dismissed by older critics, and then reshapes the whole art form.

In business or technology: An entrepreneur who disrupts an entire industry, makes enemies of established players, ignores every tradition, and is either called a visionary or a menace — often both.

Historically, figures like Jean Cocteau (the French poet, filmmaker and artist) were called enfants terribles in their own time. The label has been applied to people like Vivienne Westwood in fashion, Lars von Trier in film, and many others across cultures. The specific names matter less than the pattern: brilliant, boundary-breaking, and impossible to ignore.

The phrase follows French grammar rules even when used in English.

Singular: enfant terrible (one such person)
Plural: enfants terribles (more than one)

In English writing, it is sometimes italicised (enfant terrible) because it is a foreign phrase, and sometimes written without italics because it has become so embedded in English usage. Both are acceptable.

The enfant terrible is not the same as simply being bad-mannered, immature, or difficult for no reason. The phrase does not apply to someone who is just obnoxious or disruptive without substance.

The essential ingredient is talent combined with fearlessness. The provocation must come from a place of genuine vision. Without that, you just have a troublemaker. With it, you have an enfant terrible — someone who breaks the rules because they see possibilities that rule-followers cannot.

"At only 26, her debut film scandalized the critics and divided audiences. Some called it self-indulgent; others called it a masterpiece. Either way, she had announced herself as the enfant terrible of her generation."

Here the phrase immediately tells you: she is young, bold, controversial, rule-breaking — and talented enough that people are paying serious attention.

An enfant terrible is a brilliantly talented but deliberately provocative and unconventional person who disrupts the norms of their field — carrying the raw, unfiltered honesty of a child who says what adults are too careful to say, but channelling it into creative work that changes how people think.
5266:
To enfeeble something or someone means to make it weak, frail, or less capable than it was before. When something enfeebles a person or a thing, it strips away strength, power, or vitality — leaving behind a diminished, fragile version of what once existed.

Think of a once-vigorous athlete who, after a prolonged illness, struggles to even walk across a room. That illness has enfeebled them. The strength they had is gone, replaced by frailty and helplessness.

This is important: enfeeble does not mean merely tired or temporarily drained. It describes a more serious, often lasting reduction in capacity. Something that has been enfeebled is genuinely and significantly diminished — it has lost its vigour, its robustness, its ability to function as it once did.

There is also always a cause behind the weakening. Something actively does the enfeebling — a disease, a force, a policy, a circumstance. The weakness doesn't arise on its own; it is inflicted or brought about.

This word is remarkably versatile. It can apply to people, institutions, systems, and even abstract things like ideas or arguments.

A person physically: A long famine had so thoroughly enfeebled the survivors that many couldn't stand without support.

A person mentally: The years of isolation slowly enfeebled his mind, making it difficult for him to think clearly or retain memories.

An institution or government: Decades of corruption have enfeebled the judiciary, hollowing out its authority until it can no longer deliver justice.

A nation or economy: The prolonged civil war enfeebled the country beyond any quick recovery.

An argument or idea: Every compromise they made further enfeebled their position, until their original point had lost all its force.

So whether it is a human body, a mind, a system of government, or even a line of reasoning — all of these can be enfeebled.
How the verb works in a sentence

Enfeeble is a transitive verb, which means it always needs two things: something doing the enfeebling (the cause), and something being enfeebled (the target).

The prolonged grief enfeebled her. — Grief is the cause; she is the target.

Years of underfunding have enfeebled the public health system. — Underfunding is the cause; the health system is the target.

It is also very commonly used in the passive voice, where the focus shifts to what happened to the target rather than who caused it:

He was enfeebled by age and sorrow.

The institution has been enfeebled over decades of neglect.

Enfeeble is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual conversation — nobody says "I'm feeling a bit enfeebled today" over breakfast. It lives in serious writing: essays, literary fiction, historical accounts, formal journalism, or academic texts.

When a writer reaches for "enfeeble" instead of a simpler word like "weaken," they are usually trying to convey something weightier — a deeper, more dramatic, or more permanent loss of strength. The word carries a gravity that plain alternatives don't always have.
How it compares to similar words

Placing enfeeble among its neighbours makes its meaning sharper.

Weaken is the broad, everyday version. Enfeeble is more formal and more specific — it implies not just reduced strength, but genuine frailty and vulnerability.

Debilitate is close and is often used in medical settings to describe physical incapacity: a debilitating injury, a debilitating condition. Enfeeble can extend more naturally into non-physical territory like institutions or ideas.

Enervate means to drain someone of energy or vitality — "the relentless heat enervated the soldiers." It tends to have a mental or emotional flavour. Enfeeble, by contrast, stresses the resulting frailty more than the draining process itself.

Undermine means to erode something from within, often gradually and insidiously. You undermine confidence, authority, or a structure. Enfeeble is more direct — it simply makes something weak, without the hidden or subversive flavour of "undermine."

Sap means to slowly drain strength away — "the long siege sapped the army's morale." It suggests a gradual, draining process. Enfeeble is more formal and emphasises the resulting weakened state more than the gradual process of getting there.

Incapacitate is stronger than enfeeble. An incapacitated person is entirely unable to function. An enfeebled person is weakened and fragile, but not necessarily completely out of action.

Enfeebles (present): Chronic stress enfeebles the immune system over time.

Enfeebled (past tense / adjective): The enfeebled king handed his crown to his son. / Years of poverty had enfeebled the entire community.

Enfeebling (ongoing action): The enfeebling effects of the drought were felt across the whole region.

To enfeeble is to make someone or something significantly weaker, more frail, and less capable — and this weakening is always caused by something, whether it is disease, neglect, hardship, or any other force that drains away strength and vitality.
5267:
Enfeebled means made significantly weak — reduced in strength, power, or energy to a point where functioning properly becomes difficult.

When you call something or someone enfeebled, you are saying that they are in a weakened state, and that this weakness is noticeable, serious, and limiting. The word almost always implies that the weakness is the result of some force, process, or circumstance acting upon the person or thing — illness, age, stress, damage, hardship, and so on.

The word carries a few important layers of meaning beyond simple "weakness":

1. A decline from a better state.
Enfeebled almost always implies that the person or thing was not always this weak. There is a before and after. A young, healthy man is not enfeebled. An old man worn down by years of illness can be. The word quietly points to a loss — something that once had strength has had that strength drained away.

2. Serious, not mild, weakness.
Enfeebled is not used for minor tiredness. If you are a little tired after a short walk, you would not say you are enfeebled. The word suggests a deep, significant reduction in strength — the kind that limits what a person or thing can actually do.

3. A sense of vulnerability.
To be enfeebled is to be exposed. You are weakened to such a degree that you are less able to protect yourself, resist threats, or perform at the level you should. This gives the word a somewhat grave, serious tone.
How It Is Used — The Different Contexts

"Enfeebled" is flexible. It is not limited to physical weakness. Here's how it works across different situations:

Physical (a person's body):
This is the most common use. A person whose body has been weakened by disease, starvation, old age, or injury can be described as enfeebled.

"After months in the hospital, she emerged enfeebled, barely able to walk to the door."

The image here is of a body that has lost its former capability — someone who struggles to do things that once came easily.

Mental or intellectual:
The mind, too, can be enfeebled. When a person's ability to think clearly, reason, or remember is seriously diminished — by dementia, extreme stress, trauma, or deterioration — their mind can be described as enfeebled.

"His once-sharp mind, now enfeebled by age, struggled to follow the conversation."

Institutions, systems, and organizations:
Importantly, "enfeebled" is not limited to living beings. Governments, systems, democracies, economies, and organizations can also be enfeebled — meaning their power, authority, or effectiveness has been significantly reduced.

"Years of corruption had left the government enfeebled, unable to respond to the crisis."
"An enfeebled economy cannot support the needs of its people."

In this context, the word is describing a weakening of power, influence, or function — not physical strength, but the equivalent of it in an institutional sense.

Abstract things:
Even ideas, arguments, or forces can be described as enfeebled if they have lost their power or impact.

"The once-popular movement had become enfeebled, losing supporters month by month."

"Enfeebled" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in serious writing — journalism, literature, history, academic essays — than in everyday casual conversation. In casual speech, people are more likely to say "weak," "worn out," or "frail." But when precision and gravity are needed, "enfeebled" does a better job than these simpler words because it packs in the additional meaning of having been made weak by something.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to "enfeebled" but are not exactly the same:

  • Weak — General and broad. Just means lacking strength. No implication of decline or cause.
  • Frail — Suggests delicate, fragile weakness, often physical and often associated with old age or a thin/light build. Less often used for systems or institutions.
  • Feeble — Very similar to enfeebled but is slightly more often used for something that was always weak, or for something weak in a general sense. "Enfeebled" more specifically highlights the process of becoming weak — something acted upon it.
  • Debilitated — Very close to enfeebled. Both suggest serious weakening that limits function. "Debilitated" tends to be used more clinically (especially for illness and injury), while "enfeebled" has a slightly broader and more literary feel.
  • Diminished — Means reduced in size, importance, or power. Close, but "diminished" doesn't always suggest the same depth of weakness that "enfeebled" does.

The key thing that makes "enfeebled" precise is this combination: serious weakness + caused by something + implying a decline from a stronger state.

Imagine a mighty old lion. Once powerful, feared, and capable — now hunched, slow, and struggling to stand after years of harsh winters and wounds. That lion is enfeebled. The strength was real. Something acted on it over time. What remains is a significantly weakened version of what was once strong. That image captures exactly what the word means, whether you apply it to a human body, a mind, or an entire nation.

Enfeebled describes something — a person, body, mind, institution, or system — that has been seriously weakened, to the point where its ability to function, resist, or perform as it once did has been meaningfully reduced.
5268:
Before diving into the different uses of this word, understand this one central image, because every meaning of "enfold" comes from it:

To wrap something around something else so that the thing inside is completely enclosed, covered, and held.

Think of how a bird spreads its wings over its eggs — covering them fully, surrounding them, keeping them safe and warm. That wrapping-around-and-enclosing action is the soul of "enfold." Once you hold that image in your mind, every other meaning will make perfect sense.

1. To physically wrap or cover something

When you fold something around an object so that the object is enclosed inside, you are enfolding it.

Think of wrapping a gift. You place the gift in the centre of the paper, then fold the paper around it on all sides until the gift is hidden inside. You have enfolded the gift in paper.

She enfolded the baby in a warm blanket.

Here, the blanket is being wrapped around the baby — covering the baby completely, on all sides.

The mother bird enfolded the eggs beneath her wings.

The wings come down and around, covering and enclosing. That is enfolding.

The key detail with this meaning: the thing doing the enfolding goes around the object. It is not just placed on top. It surrounds.

2. To hold someone in your arms; to embrace

When you hug someone tightly — pulling them close and wrapping your arms fully around them — you enfold them. This is a warmer, more complete kind of embrace than a casual hug. The arms go around, they enclose. The person feels held, contained, safe.

He enfolded her in his arms and didn't let go.

She ran to her father, who enfolded her in a warm embrace.

Notice that this meaning is really just the first meaning applied to people and arms. Your arms are the "wrapping material." The person is the thing being wrapped. The result is a full, enclosing embrace.

This use of "enfold" often appears in emotional moments — reunions, comfort, love — because the word itself carries a sense of warmth and protection. It is not a cold or mechanical word.

3. To surround something completely (with something non-physical)

This is the figurative, or non-literal, use of "enfold." Here, something like darkness, silence, mist, warmth, or even a feeling "wraps itself around" a place or a person — surrounding it the same way a blanket would, even though nothing physical is actually folding.

The valley was enfolded in thick morning mist.

The mist is all around the valley — above it, inside it, on every side. Just like a blanket wraps around something, the mist has wrapped around the valley.

Darkness enfolded the forest.

The darkness has come in from all sides. There is no direction you can look and escape it. The forest is inside the darkness, the way a gift is inside wrapping paper.

A sense of calm enfolded her the moment she stepped inside.

The feeling of calm did not just touch her — it surrounded her. She was inside the calm. She was held by it.

This figurative use is very common in descriptive writing and literature. Writers use "enfold" when they want to show that something is not just nearby, but completely surrounding and immersing a person or a place.

4. To include or absorb something into a larger whole

This is the least common meaning but worth knowing. When something is brought into a group, a system, or a whole — absorbed and contained within it — it can be said to be enfolded into it.

The small company was enfolded into the larger organisation.

The small company did not just join — it was brought in and absorbed. It is now inside the larger body, the way something small is enclosed inside a fold.

These ideas were gradually enfolded into the main philosophy of the movement.

Again, the ideas went inside, became part of, were surrounded by and contained within the larger thing.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Enfold" is not a neutral, flat word. It carries warmth, gentleness, and a sense of protection. When something is enfolded, it is not just covered — it is held. It is safe. It is surrounded with care.

Compare these two sentences:

  • He wrapped his arms around her.
  • He enfolded her in his arms.

Both describe the same action. But the second one feels more tender, more complete, more protective. "Enfold" suggests the person is truly inside the arms — enclosed, held — not just touched by them.

This is why "enfold" appears often in poetry, literary fiction, and emotional descriptions. It is a word that does not just describe an action — it describes the feeling of that action.

Understanding what typically does the enfolding and what typically gets enfolded will help you use the word naturally.

Things that enfold:
Arms, wings, blankets, fabric, darkness, mist, fog, silence, warmth, love, grief, calm, sleep, a crowd, an organisation, a philosophy.

Things that get enfolded:
A person, a baby, an object, a valley, a city, a forest, an idea, a smaller group.

Common patterns:

  • enfold someone/something in something — "She enfolded the child in her arms."
  • be enfolded in/by something — "The town was enfolded in silence."
  • enfold someone/something — "Darkness enfolded them."

You may know words like wrap, cover, surround, embrace, and hug. "Enfold" is close to all of them, but it is not identical.

Enfold vs. Wrap: "Wrap" is more practical and physical. You wrap a package. "Enfold" is more complete and often warmer in tone — it suggests going fully around and holding, not just covering.

Enfold vs. Hug/Embrace: A hug can be quick and light. "Enfold" suggests a fuller, closer, more enclosing kind of embrace — the arms go fully around and hold.

Enfold vs. Surround: "Surround" is neutral and can be threatening (soldiers surrounded the building). "Enfold" is almost always gentle and warm. You are not just around something — you are holding it.

Enfold vs. Cover: "Cover" means something goes on top. "Enfold" means something goes all the way around, on all sides.

"Enfold" as a verb means to wrap something completely around something else — physically or figuratively — so that it is enclosed, surrounded, and held. It can describe arms wrapping around a person, fabric wrapping around an object, or something non-physical like darkness or silence completely surrounding a place or a person. It can also describe a smaller thing being absorbed into a larger whole. Across all these uses, the word carries a consistent sense of warmth, completeness, and gentle containment.
5269:
To enfranchise means to grant someone a right, freedom, or power that they were previously denied. It is about letting people in — into a system, a process, or a society — after they had been locked out of it.

Think of it this way: imagine a room where important decisions are made. Some people are allowed inside; others are kept at the door. To enfranchise someone is to open that door for them and say, "You belong here too."
The Most Common and Specific Meaning — The Right to Vote

In everyday use, enfranchise almost always refers to granting the right to vote. When a government enfranchises a group of people, it officially gives them the legal right to participate in elections — something they could not do before.

For example:

  • The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution enfranchised women in 1920, meaning women gained the right to vote for the first time.
  • For centuries, poor people who didn't own land were not enfranchised — they had no say in who governed them.
  • Many civil rights movements throughout history fought to enfranchise Black citizens, Indigenous people, and other groups who were deliberately excluded from voting.

So when you see or hear "enfranchise" in a political or historical context, it almost certainly means: giving someone the right to vote.
The Broader Meaning — General Freedom and Empowerment

Beyond voting, enfranchise is also used more broadly to mean giving someone the freedom, power, or means to participate fully in something — to have a real voice, a real stake, a real place.

In this wider sense, it means removing whatever barrier was keeping someone powerless or excluded.

For example:

  • A company that gives its employees a role in decision-making is enfranchising its workers — it is giving them a genuine voice rather than just taking orders.
  • Access to quality education can enfranchise people from poor backgrounds by equipping them to engage with opportunities that were previously out of reach.
  • A new law that allows people with disabilities to access public spaces more easily enfranchises them — it brings them into full participation in society.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: someone who was excluded, overlooked, or powerless is now being given access, rights, or real influence.
The Historical Meaning — Freedom from Slavery or Bondage

In older and historical texts, enfranchise was used to mean setting someone free from slavery, serfdom, or other forms of bondage. A slave who was formally freed, or a serf released from obligation to a lord, was said to be enfranchised.

This meaning is rarely used in modern English, but you may encounter it when reading historical documents or literature from earlier centuries.
One More Historical Usage — Towns and Boroughs

In British political history, enfranchise was also used to mean granting a town or borough the right to send elected representatives to Parliament. Just as a person could be enfranchised, so could a place — meaning it was brought into the political system for the first time.

Again, this is historical and specific, and you are unlikely to encounter it in modern conversation, but it is worth knowing.

Every time you see enfranchise, keep its opposite in mind: disenfranchise (sometimes written as disfranchise).

To disenfranchise someone is to take away their rights — especially their right to vote — or to make them feel so powerless and excluded that their participation becomes meaningless even if technically permitted.

For example:

  • Voter suppression tactics disenfranchise communities by making it harder for them to cast their votes.
  • A government that ignores its citizens completely disenfranchises them — their voices count for nothing in practice.

The two words are mirror images of each other: enfranchise opens the door, disenfranchise shuts it.
How the Word is Used in Practice

A few things to note about how this word behaves in sentences:

It is a formal word. You will mostly see and hear it in political writing, journalism, history, law, and serious social commentary. It is not casual conversation language.

It often appears in the passive voice. Rather than saying "The government enfranchised women," people very commonly say "Women were enfranchised in 1920." Both are correct, and you should be comfortable reading both forms.

It always implies a power relationship. There is always someone granting the right and someone receiving it. Enfranchisement is given by those in authority — a government, an institution, a system — to those who had been excluded from it. The people being enfranchised could not simply give themselves this status; it required formal recognition.

It implies previous exclusion. You do not enfranchise someone who already had rights. The word only makes sense when there was a previous state of being shut out.

If you want one clean summary to anchor everything:

To enfranchise is to formally grant someone — especially a group that was previously excluded — the right to participate in a process or system. Most commonly, this means the right to vote. More broadly, it means giving someone genuine freedom, power, or a real voice where they had none before. Its opposite is disenfranchise — to take those rights away, or to render someone's participation meaningless.

The word carries weight. It belongs to serious conversations about justice, power, and who gets to have a say in the world around them.
